title: Notation
body_md: $\|x\|$ is the Euclidean norm of a vector and $\|A\|$ the operator norm of a matrix; $\lambda_{\min}(A)$, $\lambda_{\max}(A)$ are the extreme eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and $\sigma_{\min}(A)$ the smallest singular value; $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semi-definite; $I_d$ is the $d\times d$ identity. For a closed set $\mathcal S$ of matrices, $\operatorname{dist}(A,\mathcal S)=\min_{B\in\mathcal S}\|A-B\|$. Convergence in distribution is denoted by $\Rightarrow$.
head: manual

label: ex:linear
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:linear}
Let $X=(y,x,z)$ with $y=x^{\top}\beta^*+u$, $\mathbb{E}[zu]=0$, where some components of $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\beta}$ are correlated with $u$ and $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_g}$ is a vector of instruments. Then $g(X,\beta)=z(x^{\top}\beta-y)$, $G(X,\beta)=zx^{\top}$ does not depend on $\beta$, and $\bar G=\mathbb{E}[zx^{\top}]$ has full column rank under the usual relevance condition. With $W=\mathbb{E}[zz^{\top}]^{-1}$, \eqref{eq:sandwich} is the asymptotic variance of 2SLS; under heteroskedasticity the efficient GMM estimator is in general more efficient.
head: environment
name: Linear IV regression

label: ex:nonlinear
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:nonlinear}
More generally let $g(X,\beta)=z\,r(X,\beta)$ for a scalar residual $r$. Examples are the additive model $y=f(x,\beta^*)+u$ with $\mathbb{E}[zu]=0$, where $r=f(x,\beta)-y$, and the multiplicative exponential model for non-negative or count outcomes, $y=\exp(x^{\top}\beta^*)\eta$ with $\mathbb{E}[\eta\mid z]=1$ \cite{Mullahy1997,WindmeijerSantosSilva1997}, where
\[
r(X,\beta)=y\,e^{-x^{\top}\beta}-1,\qquad \partial_\beta r(X,\beta)=-y\,e^{-x^{\top}\beta}x .
\]
In both cases the Jacobian $G(X,\beta)=z\,\partial_\beta r(X,\beta)^{\top}$ has rank one, which is exploited in Lemma~\ref{lem:woodbury}. The linear model of Example~\ref{ex:linear} is the special case $r=x^{\top}\beta-y$.

head: environment

label: rem:design
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:design}
(i) The parameter step uses the current iterate $\beta_{i-1}$, while the Jacobian and the weight matrix are evaluated at the averaged iterate $\bar\beta_{i-1}$, which is less noisy; both are $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable, where $\mathcal{F}_i$ is generated by the pilot sample and $X_1,\dots,X_i$, so that every update is driven by a martingale difference. This is the convention of the nonlinear SGMM of \citet[Section~7]{ChenEtAl2025}; for their linear efficient SGMM they compute the weight at a fixed preliminary estimate instead.
(ii) By construction $\Phi_i=(n_0+i)^{-1}\big(n_0\Phi_0+\sum_{j=1}^iG(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})\big)$ and $W_i=S_i^{-1}$ with $S_i=(n_0+i)^{-1}\big(n_0S_0+\sum_{j=1}^is_js_j^{\top}\big)$; line~6 is the Sherman--Morrison formula for this inverse (Lemma~\ref{lem:woodbury}(a)).
(iii) The projection and the truncation are needed for the proofs; they are inactive after a finite random time (Theorem~\ref{thm:as}). If $\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\Phi_i$ is singular, which almost surely happens only finitely often (Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}), the step is skipped and $H_i$ is computed directly once the matrix becomes invertible. In our simulations of independent data the truncation and the projection onto a large box were never active for SGMM with the default steps of (v) below (they were for the first-order version in rescaled units; Section~\ref{sec:sens}).
(iv) Replacing $s_i$ by the instrument vector $z_i$ in line~6 yields $W_i\to\mathbb{E}[zz^{\top}]^{-1}$ and the online 2SLS estimator of \citet{ChenEtAl2025} in the linear case (Remark~\ref{rem:2sls}).
(v) \emph{Default steps.} We use $a=3/4$, $i_0=n_0$ and $\gamma_0=c_\gamma n_0^{a-1}$, i.e.\ $\gamma_i=c_\gamma n_0^{a-1}(n_0+i)^{-a}$ with $c_\gamma=2$. The first step is then $\gamma_1\approx c_\gamma/n_0$, the weight of one additional observation in a recursive estimate based on the $n_0$ pilot observations, and the steps continue to decrease as $(n_0+i)^{-a}$. This rule needs no tuning to the scale of the problem, because the Gauss--Newton step is invariant to invertible linear reparametrizations of $\beta$ and of the moments, apart from the effect of the ridge $\eta_0$ and of the projection (Section~\ref{sec:sens}). It matters most when some parameters are weakly identified, so that single observations produce large Gauss--Newton steps: in the application of Section~\ref{sec:application}, larger first steps ($i_0=100$, $\gamma_0=1$) left the final estimates more than three standard errors away from the offline estimates in all $20$ orderings of the data. The offset $i_0=n_0$ also damps the first steps, in which a single observation would otherwise move the iterate by almost a full Gauss--Newton step.

name: Recursive inversion

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) is the Sherman--Morrison formula applied to $NS_{i-1}+ss^{\top}$, whose inverse is $N^{-1}W-N^{-2}Wss^{\top} W/(1+N^{-1}s^{\top} Ws)=N^{-1}(W-Wss^{\top} W/\ell)$, multiplied by $N+1$.

(b) Put $A=N\Phi+z\psi^{\top}$, so that $\Phi_i=A/(N+1)$ and, by (a), $W_i=(N+1)(NS_{i-1}+ss^{\top})^{-1}=\frac{N+1}{N}(W-Wss^{\top} W/\ell)$, where $s^{\top} Ws=\varrho^2c_z$. Hence
\[
\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\Phi_i=\frac{1}{N(N+1)}\Big(A^{\top} WA-\frac1\ell(A^{\top} Ws)(A^{\top} Ws)^{\top}\Big).
\]
Now $A^{\top} WA=N^2\Phi^{\top} W\Phi+N(u\psi^{\top}+\psi u^{\top})+c_z\psi\psi^{\top}$ and $A^{\top} Ws=\varrho(Nu+c_z\psi)$, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^{\top} WA-\frac{(A^{\top} Ws)(A^{\top} Ws)^{\top}}{\ell}&=N^2\Phi^{\top} W\Phi+N\Big(1-\frac{\varrho^2c_z}{\ell}\Big)(u\psi^{\top}+\psi u^{\top})\\&\quad-\frac{N^2\varrho^2}{\ell}uu^{\top}+c_z\Big(1-\frac{\varrho^2c_z}{\ell}\Big)\psi\psi^{\top}\\
&=N^2\Phi^{\top} W\Phi+N\,U\mathcal CU^{\top} ,
\end{aligned}
\]
because $1-\varrho^2c_z/\ell=N/\ell$ and $U\mathcal CU^{\top}=\ell^{-1}\big(-N\varrho^2uu^{\top}+N(u\psi^{\top}+\psi u^{\top})+c_z\psi\psi^{\top}\big)$. Therefore $(N+1)\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\Phi_i=N\,\Phi^{\top} W\Phi+U\mathcal CU^{\top}$. For an invertible matrix $B$ and any $U$, $\mathcal C$ such that $B+U\mathcal CU^{\top}$ is invertible, the matrix $I+\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}U$ is invertible and
\[
(B+U\mathcal CU^{\top})^{-1}=B^{-1}-B^{-1}U(I+\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}U)^{-1}\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}.
\]
Indeed, if $(I+\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}U)v=0$, then $w=B^{-1}Uv$ satisfies $(B+U\mathcal CU^{\top})w=U(I+\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}U)v=0$, so $w=0$, hence $Uv=Bw=0$ and $v=-\mathcal CU^{\top} B^{-1}Uv=0$; the identity is then verified by multiplying the right-hand side by $B+U\mathcal CU^{\top}$. With $B=N\Phi^{\top} W\Phi$, $B^{-1}=H/N$, this gives \eqref{eq:woodbury3}.

(c) For $\varrho=1$, $\ell=N+c_z$ and, expanding the right-hand side and using $1-N/\ell=c_z/\ell$,
\[
\begin{aligned}U\mathcal CU^{\top}&=\frac1\ell\big(-Nuu^{\top}+N(u\psi^{\top}+\psi u^{\top})+c_z\psi\psi^{\top}\big)\\&=-\frac{N}{\ell}(\psi-u)(\psi-u)^{\top}+\psi\psi^{\top}=U_2\tilde{\mathcal C}U_2^{\top},\qquad\tilde{\mathcal C}=\operatorname{diag}(-N/\ell,1).\end{aligned}
\]
Hence $(N+1)\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\Phi_i=NH^{-1}+U_2\tilde{\mathcal C}U_2^{\top}$, and the classical Woodbury identity
\[
\big(NH^{-1}+U_2\tilde{\mathcal C}U_2^{\top}\big)^{-1}=\frac1N\Big(H-HU_2\big(N\tilde{\mathcal C}^{-1}+U_2^{\top} HU_2\big)^{-1}U_2^{\top} H\Big),\qquad N\tilde{\mathcal C}^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(-\ell,N)=D,
\]
gives \eqref{eq:woodbury2}; the $2\times2$ matrix $D+U_2^{\top} HU_2$ is invertible by the argument of part (b).

label: ass:data
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:data}
$X_1,X_2,\dots$ are i.i.d.\ copies of $X$ and independent of $\mathcal{F}_0$. The set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_\beta}$ is compact and convex, $\beta^*$ lies in its interior, $n_0\ged_\beta$, and $\beta_0\in\Theta$, $\Phi_0$ and the positive definite $S_0$ are $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable.
head: environment
name: Data and parameter space

label: ass:smooth
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:smooth}
For every $\beta$, $x\mapsto g(x,\beta)$ is measurable, and for every $x$, $\beta\mapsto g(x,\beta)$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $\mathcal O\supset\Theta$. Let $B(x)=\sup_{\beta\in\Theta}\|g(x,\beta)\|+\sup_{\beta\in\Theta}\|G(x,\beta)\|$. There is a measurable $L$ with $\|G(x,\beta)-G(x,\beta')\|\le L(x)\|\beta-\beta'\|$ for $\beta,\beta'\in\Theta$, and $\mathbb{E}[B(X)^\kappa]<\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[L(X)]<\infty$ for some $\kappa\ge4$. Moreover $\lambda_0=\inf_{\beta\in\Theta}\lambda_{\min}(\Omega(\beta))>0$ and $G^*$ has full column rank $d_\beta$.

label: ass:mono
title: Assumption

There are $\delta_\Phi,\sigma_0,c>0$ such that every $\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d_g\timesd_\beta}$ with $\operatorname{dist}(\Phi,\mathcal G)\le\delta_\Phi$ satisfies $\sigma_{\min}(\Phi)\ge\sigma_0$, and

\big\langle\beta-\beta^*,\,P(\Phi,W)\,m(\beta)\big\rangle\ge c\,\|\beta-\beta^*\|^2\qquad\text{for all }\beta\in\Theta,\ W\in\mathcal W,\ \operatorname{dist}(\Phi,\mathcal G)\le\delta_\Phi,

body_md:
\label{cor:datadriven}
Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:smooth} holds on $\Theta_0=\bar B(\beta^*,r_0)$, let $r_1$ be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:local}(a), $0<\rho\le r_1/2$, and let $\Theta=\bar B(\hat\beta_{\rm pilot},\rho)$ for an $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable pilot estimator. label: thm:as
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:as}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:data}--\ref{ass:steps}, $\beta_n\to\beta^*$ and $\bar\beta_n\to\beta^*$ almost surely. Moreover, almost surely, $\Phi_n\to G^*$, $W_n\to\Omega^{*-1}$, $H_n\to\Sigma^*=(G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}G^*)^{-1}$ and $P_n\to P^*=\Sigma^*G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}$, and there is a finite random time after which neither the truncation nor the projection is active.

body_md:
\label{thm:rate}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:data}--\ref{ass:steps}, for every $\varepsilon>(1-a)/\kappa$,
\[
\|\beta_n-\beta^*\|=O\big(n^{-a/2+\varepsilon}\big),\qquad\|\bar\beta_n-\beta^*\|=O\big(n^{-a/2+\varepsilon}\big),\qquad \|\Phi_n-G^*\|+\|W_n-\Omega^{*-1}\|=O\big(n^{-a/2+\varepsilon}\big)
\]

label: cor:inference
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:inference}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),itemsep=2pt]
\item $H_n\to\Sigma^*$ almost surely, and for every $k\led_\beta$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ the interval $\bar\beta_{n,k}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{H_{n,kk}/n}$ has asymptotic coverage $1-\alpha$.
\item (Random scaling.) Let $V_n=n^{-2}\sum_{s=1}^ns^2(\bar\beta_s-\bar\beta_n)(\bar\beta_s-\bar\beta_n)^{\top}$. Then
\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\bar\beta_{n,k}-\beta^*_k)}{\sqrt{V_{n,kk}}}\Rightarrow\frac{\mathbf b(1)}{\big(\int_0^1(\mathbf b(r)-r\mathbf b(1))^2\,\mathrm{d} r\big)^{1/2}},
\]
with $\mathbf b$ a standard Brownian motion. The limit is pivotal and symmetric, with distribution tabulated by \citet{AbadirParuolo1997} and \citet{KieferVogelsangBunzel2000}; the two-sided $95\%$ critical value is $6.747$ \cite{LeeLiaoSeoShin2022}.
\end{enumerate}

Suppose the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt} hold and $d_g>d_\beta$. Then $\sqrt n\big(\hat g_n-\bar g_n(\bar\beta_n)\big)\to0$ almost surely, and $\mathcal J_n\Rightarrow\chi^2_{d_g-d_\beta}$.

label: ass:ldep
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:ldep}
The sequence $(X_i)_{i>-n_0}$ (pilot sample and stream) is strictly stationary and $L$-dependent for some known $L\ge0$: $\sigma(X_j,\,j\le i)$ is independent of $\sigma(X_j,\,j\ge i+L+1)$ for every $i$. The long-run second-moment matrix $\Omega_{\rm LR}(\beta)=\sum_{h=-L}^{L}\mathbb{E}\big[g(X_0,\beta)g(X_h,\beta)^{\top}\big]$ satisfies $\inf_{\beta\in\Theta}\lambda_{\min}(\Omega_{\rm LR}(\beta))>0$.

name: $L$-dependent data

label: thm:dependent
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dependent}
Replace the independence condition in Assumption~\ref{ass:data} by Assumption~\ref{ass:ldep}, the conditions on $\Theta$, $n_0$, $\beta_0$, $\Phi_0$ and $S_0$ remaining in force. Define $\lambda_0$, $\Lambda$ and $\mathcal W$ with $\Omega_{\rm LR}$ in place of $\Omega$, and use the weights \eqref{eq:lrv}. Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:smooth}--\ref{ass:steps} and $\kappa>2/(2a-1)$, the conclusions of Theorems~\ref{thm:as} and~\ref{thm:rate} hold with $\Omega^*$ replaced by $\Omega^*_{\rm LR}=\Omega_{\rm LR}(\beta^*)$, the latter for every $\varepsilon>\max\{(1-a)/\kappa,\,2/\kappa-a/2,\,3/\kappa-1+a/2\}$. If moreover $\kappa>\kappa_L(a)$, the conclusions of Theorems~\ref{thm:fclt} and~\ref{thm:J} and of Corollary~\ref{cor:inference} hold with $\Omega^*$ replaced by $\Omega^*_{\rm LR}$. In particular $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*)\Rightarrow N\big(0,(G^{*\top}\Omega_{\rm LR}^{*-1}G^*)^{-1}\big)$, which is the efficient GMM variance under $L$-dependence, $H_n$ estimates it consistently, and $\mathcal J_n\Rightarrow\chi^2_{d_g-d_\beta}$.

label: lem:weights
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weights}
Let $\gamma_i$ be as in Assumption~\ref{ass:steps} and $\Gamma_{k,i}=\prod_{j=k+1}^i(1-\gamma_j)$, with $\Gamma_{i,i}=1$. There is $i_1$ such that $\gamma_j\le1/2$ for $j\ge i_1$. For $i\ge k\ge i_1$, $0\le\Gamma_{k,i}\le\exp(-\sum_{j=k+1}^i\gamma_j)$ and $\sum_{k=i_1}^i\gamma_k^2\Gamma_{k,i}^2\le C\gamma_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\gamma_j\to0$, there is $i_1$ with $\gamma_j\le1/2$ for $j\ge i_1$. Every factor of $\Gamma_{k,i}$ then lies in $[1/2,1)$, so $\Gamma_{k,i}\ge0$, and $1-x\le e^{-x}$ gives the first bound. For the second, let $u_i=\sum_{k=i_1}^i\gamma_k^2\Gamma_{k,i}^2$. Since $\Gamma_{k,i}=(1-\gamma_i)\Gamma_{k,i-1}$ for $k<i$ and $\Gamma_{i,i}=1$,
\[
u_i=(1-\gamma_i)^2u_{i-1}+\gamma_i^2\le(1-\gamma_i)u_{i-1}+\gamma_i^2 .
\]
By the mean value theorem, $\gamma_{i-1}-\gamma_i=\gamma_0\big((i+i_0-1)^{-a}-(i+i_0)^{-a}\big)\le a\gamma_{i-1}/(i+i_0-1)$. Since $a<1$, we have $\gamma_{i-1}/\big((i+i_0-1)\gamma_i^2\big)\to0$. Hence $a\gamma_{i-1}/(i+i_0-1)\le\gamma_i^2/2$ for all $i$ larger than some $i_2\ge i_1$. Using $\gamma_i\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i^2$, this gives
\[
\gamma_{i-1}-\gamma_i-\gamma_i\gamma_{i-1}\le-\gamma_i^2/2\qquad(i>i_2).
\]
Choose $C\ge2$ with $u_i\le C\gamma_i$ for $i_1\le i\le i_2$. If $i>i_2$ and $u_{i-1}\le C\gamma_{i-1}$, then
\[
u_i\le(1-\gamma_i)C\gamma_{i-1}+\gamma_i^2=C\gamma_i+C(\gamma_{i-1}-\gamma_i-\gamma_i\gamma_{i-1})+\gamma_i^2\le C\gamma_i-(C/2-1)\gamma_i^2\le C\gamma_i ,
\]
and the claim follows by induction.

label: lem:det
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:det}
Let $u_i\ge0$ satisfy $u_i\le(1-\gamma_i/2)u_{i-1}+\gamma_i\eta_iv_{i-1}$ for $i>i_3$, where $i_3$ is finite (possibly random), $\eta_i\to0$, and $v_i=i^{-q}$ with $0<q<1$. Then $u_i=o(v_i)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varsigma_i=u_i/v_i\ge0$. Since $(1+x)^q\le1+qx$ for $x\ge0$ and $i\gamma_i\to\infty$, there is $i_4\ge i_3$ such that for $i>i_4$
\[
\frac{v_{i-1}}{v_i}=\Big(1+\frac1{i-1}\Big)^q\le1+\frac{2q}{i}\le1+\frac{\gamma_i}4\qquad\text{and}\qquad\gamma_i\le1 .
\]
Dividing the recursion by $v_i$ and using $(1-x/2)(1+x/4)=1-x/4-x^2/8$, we get for $i>i_4$
\[
\varsigma_i\le(1-\gamma_i/2)(1+\gamma_i/4)\varsigma_{i-1}+\gamma_i\eta_i(1+\gamma_i/4)\le(1-\gamma_i/4)\varsigma_{i-1}+2\gamma_i|\eta_i| .
\]
Fix $\theta>0$ and $i_5\ge i_4$ with $|\eta_i|\le\theta$ for $i>i_5$. Then $\varsigma_i-8\theta\le(1-\gamma_i/4)(\varsigma_{i-1}-8\theta)$, and hence $(\varsigma_i-8\theta)^+\le(1-\gamma_i/4)(\varsigma_{i-1}-8\theta)^+$, for $i>i_5$. Iterating,
\[
(\varsigma_i-8\theta)^+\le(\varsigma_{i_5}-8\theta)^+\exp\Big(-\frac14\sum_{j=i_5+1}^i\gamma_j\Big)\to0,
\]
because $\sum_j\gamma_j=\infty$. Thus $\limsup_i\varsigma_i\le8\theta$ for every $\theta>0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(b) By Remark~\ref{rem:design}(ii),
\[
\Phi_i=\frac{n_0}{n_0+i}\Phi_0+\frac{1}{n_0+i}\sum_{j=1}^i\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})+\frac{1}{n_0+i}M^\Phi_i,\qquad M^\Phi_i=\sum_{j=1}^i\Delta^\Phi_j,\quad\Delta^\Phi_j=G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})-\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1}).
\]
The point $\bar\beta_{j-1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}$-measurable, and $X_j$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}$ with the distribution of $X$. Therefore $\mathbb{E}[G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]=\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})$, so the $\Delta^\Phi_j$ are martingale differences, with $\mathbb{E}\|\Delta_j^\Phi\|^2\le2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]+2\big(\mathbb{E} B(X)\big)^2\le4\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]$. By (T2), $M^\Phi_i=O(i^{1/2+\varepsilon'})$ almost surely. Since $\frac{1}{n_0+i}-\frac1i=-\frac{n_0}{i(n_0+i)}$ and $\|\bar G(\beta)\|\le\mathbb{E} B(X)$,
\[
\Big\|\Phi_i-\frac1i\sum_{j\le i}\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})\Big\|\le\frac{n_0}{n_0+i}\big(\|\Phi_0\|+\mathbb{E} B(X)\big)+\frac{\|M_i^\Phi\|}{n_0+i}=O\big(i^{-1/2+\varepsilon'}\big).
\]
The same argument applies to $S_i=(n_0+i)^{-1}\big(n_0S_0+\sum_{j\le i}s_js_j^{\top}\big)$, with $\Omega(\bar\beta_{j-1})$ in place of $\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})$ and martingale differences $s_js_j^{\top}-\Omega(\bar\beta_{j-1})$. Their second moments are at most $2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^4]+2\|\Omega(\bar\beta_{j-1})\|^2\le4\mathbb{E}[B(X)^4]<\infty$, since $\kappa\ge4$.

(a) Let $\bar G_i^{\rm av}=i^{-1}\sum_{j\le i}\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})$ and $\Omega_i^{\rm av}=i^{-1}\sum_{j\le i}\Omega(\bar\beta_{j-1})$. Since $\bar\beta_{j-1}\in\Theta$, $\bar G_i^{\rm av}$ is a convex combination of elements of $\{\bar G(\beta):\beta\in\Theta\}$, so $\bar G_i^{\rm av}\in\mathcal G$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_i,\mathcal G)\le\|\Phi_i-\bar G_i^{\rm av}\|\to0$ by (b). The function $\lambda_{\min}$ is concave and $\lambda_{\max}$ is convex on symmetric matrices, so the eigenvalues of $\Omega_i^{\rm av}$ lie in $[\lambda_0,\Lambda]$. By Weyl's inequality, $|\lambda_k(S_i)-\lambda_k(\Omega_i^{\rm av})|\le\|S_i-\Omega_i^{\rm av}\|\to0$ for every $k$. Hence the eigenvalues of $S_i$ lie in $[\lambda_0/2,2\Lambda]$ for $i$ large, and those of $W_i=S_i^{-1}$ lie in $[(2\Lambda)^{-1},2\lambda_0^{-1}]$.

(c) If $\bar\beta_i\to\beta^*$, continuity of $\bar G$ and $\Omega$ gives $\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})\to G^*$ and $\Omega(\bar\beta_{j-1})\to\Omega^*$. Hence $\bar G_i^{\rm av}\to G^*$ and $\Omega_i^{\rm av}\to\Omega^*$ by Ces\`aro's lemma, and $\Phi_i\to G^*$, $S_i\to\Omega^*$ by (b). Matrix inversion is continuous on invertible matrices, so $W_i\to\Omega^{*-1}$. The matrix $G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}G^*$ is invertible because $G^*$ has full column rank and $\Omega^{*-1}$ is positive definite. Hence $\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\Phi_i$ is invertible for $i$ large, $H_i\to\Sigma^*$ and $P(\Phi_i,W_i)=H_i\Phi_i^{\top} W_i\to P^*$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) For a compact convex $\Theta\subseteq\Theta_0$, let $\lambda_0(\Theta)$, $\Lambda(\Theta)$, $\mathcal W_\Theta$ and $\mathcal G_\Theta$ be the quantities of Section~\ref{sec:theory} computed on $\Theta$. Since $\lambda_0(\Theta)\ge\lambda_0(\Theta_0)$ and $\Lambda(\Theta)\le\Lambda(\Theta_0)$, we have $\mathcal W_\Theta\subseteq\mathcal W_{\Theta_0}$. Every $W\in\mathcal W_{\Theta_0}$ has condition number at most $k_W=4\Lambda(\Theta_0)/\lambda_0(\Theta_0)$. Let $\sigma^*=\sigma_{\min}(G^*)>0$. Take $\delta_\Phi>0$ and $r_1\in(0,r_0]$ with $\delta_\Phi+\bar Lr_1\le\sigma^*/2$, and let $\Theta\subseteq\bar B(\beta^*,r_1)$ with $\beta^*\in\operatorname{int}\Theta$.

Since $\bar G$ is $\bar L$-Lipschitz, $\mathcal G_\Theta\subseteq\bar B(G^*,\bar Lr_1)$. So if $\operatorname{dist}(\Phi,\mathcal G_\Theta)\le\delta_\Phi$, then $\|\Phi-G^*\|\le\delta_\Phi+\bar Lr_1\le\sigma^*/2$. By Weyl's inequality for singular values, $\sigma_{\min}(\Phi)\ge\sigma^*/2=:\sigma_0$, and $\|\Phi\|\le\|G^*\|+\sigma_0$. As in \eqref{eq:Pbound}, $\|(\Phi^{\top} W\Phi)^{-1}\|\le1/(\lambda_{\min}(W)\sigma_{\min}(\Phi)^2)$, so for $W\in\mathcal W_\Theta$
\[
\|P(\Phi,W)\|\le\frac{\lambda_{\max}(W)\|\Phi\|}{\lambda_{\min}(W)\sigma_{\min}(\Phi)^2}\le\frac{k_W(\|G^*\|+\sigma_0)}{\sigma_0^2}=:p_0 .
\]
For $\beta\in\Theta$, the segment from $\beta^*$ to $\beta$ lies in $\Theta\subseteq\mathcal O$. Hence $g(x,\beta)-g(x,\beta^*)=\int_0^1G(x,\beta^*+t(\beta-\beta^*))\,\mathrm{d} t\,(\beta-\beta^*)$. Since $\|G\|\le B$ is integrable and $m(\beta^*)=0$, Fubini's theorem gives
\begin{gather*}
m(\beta)=\tilde G(\beta)(\beta-\beta^*),\qquad\tilde G(\beta)=\int_0^1\bar G\big(\beta^*+t(\beta-\beta^*)\big)\,\mathrm{d} t,\\ \|\tilde G(\beta)-G^*\|\le\int_0^1\bar Lt\|\beta-\beta^*\|\,\mathrm{d} t\le\frac{\bar Lr_1}2 .
\end{gather*}
Using $P(\Phi,W)\Phi=I$,
\[
P(\Phi,W)m(\beta)=(\beta-\beta^*)+P(\Phi,W)\big(\tilde G(\beta)-\Phi\big)(\beta-\beta^*),\qquad\|\tilde G(\beta)-\Phi\|\le\frac{\bar Lr_1}2+\delta_\Phi+\bar Lr_1 .
\]
Hence $\langle\beta-\beta^*,P(\Phi,W)m(\beta)\rangle\ge\big(1-p_0(\delta_\Phi+2\bar Lr_1)\big)\|\beta-\beta^*\|^2$. Choosing $\delta_\Phi$ and $r_1$ smaller if necessary, so that $p_0(\delta_\Phi+2\bar Lr_1)\le1/2$, gives the claim with $c=1/2$. Here $p_0$ depends only on $\Theta_0$ and $\sigma_0=\sigma^*/2$, so the constants $\delta_\Phi$, $\sigma_0$ and $c$ do not depend on $\Theta$.

(b) In the linear model, $\bar G\equiv G^*$, $\mathcal G=\{G^*\}$ and $m(\beta)=G^*(\beta-\beta^*)$ on all of $\mathbb{R}^{d_\beta}$. The argument of (a) applies with $\bar L=0$, $\Theta_0=\Theta$ and no restriction on $r_1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
On $\mathcal E_\rho$, every $\beta\in\Theta$ satisfies $\|\beta-\beta^*\|\le\|\beta-\hat\beta_{\rm pilot}\|+\|\hat\beta_{\rm pilot}-\beta^*\|<2\rho\le r_1$. The open ball around $\beta^*$ of radius $\rho-\|\hat\beta_{\rm pilot}-\beta^*\|>0$ is contained in $\Theta$, so $\beta^*\in\operatorname{int}\Theta$.

Let $\mathcal P$ denote the pilot sample. All inputs of Algorithm~\ref{alg:sgmm} that depend on $\mathcal P$ are measurable functions of it: $\Theta$, $\beta_0$, $\Phi_0$ and $S_0$. The iterates are therefore measurable functions of $(\mathcal P,X_1,X_2,\dots)$. Fix a value $p$ of $\mathcal P$ with $\|\hat\beta_{\rm pilot}(p)-\beta^*\|<\rho$, and run the algorithm on the stream $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ with the deterministic inputs $\Theta(p)$, $\beta_0(p)$, $\Phi_0(p)$, $S_0(p)$. Assumption~\ref{ass:data} holds. Assumption~\ref{ass:smooth} holds on $\Theta(p)\subseteq\Theta_0$, because the envelope $B$ and the Lipschitz function $L$ computed over $\Theta(p)$ are bounded by those computed over $\Theta_0$, and $\lambda_0(\Theta(p))\ge\lambda_0(\Theta_0)>0$. Assumption~\ref{ass:mono} holds by Proposition~\ref{prop:local}(a), and Assumption~\ref{ass:steps} does not involve $p$. Hence the conclusions of Theorems~\ref{thm:as}--\ref{thm:J} hold for this deterministic input, under the respective moment conditions.

Since $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ is independent of $\mathcal P$, Fubini's theorem gives, for every measurable event $A$ of the form $\{(\mathcal P,(X_i)_{i\ge1})\in\mathcal A\}$, $\mathbb{P}(A)=\int\mathbb{P}\big((p,(X_i)_{i\ge1})\in\mathcal A\big)\,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal P}(\,\mathrm{d} p)$. With $A=\{\bar\beta_n\to\beta^*\}$, the integrand equals one whenever $\|\hat\beta_{\rm pilot}(p)-\beta^*\|<\rho$, so $\mathbb{P}(\bar\beta_n\to\beta^*)\ge\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_\rho)$. The distributional conclusions hold in the same way under the conditional distribution given $\mathcal P=p$, for such $p$. If the pilot estimator is consistent as $n_0\to\infty$, then $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_\rho)\to1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: eventual regime.} Define the $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable event
\[
E_{i-1}=\big\{\Phi_{i-1}\in\mathcal N,\ W_{i-1}\in\mathcal W,\ P_{i-1}=P(\Phi_{i-1},W_{i-1})\big\}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}(a), almost surely $\Phi_{i-1}\in\mathcal N$ and $W_{i-1}\in\mathcal W$ for all $i$ large. Then $\Phi_{i-1}^{\top} W_{i-1}\Phi_{i-1}$ is invertible and $\|P(\Phi_{i-1},W_{i-1})\|\le p_{\max}$ by \eqref{eq:Pbound}. Since $\bar p_i\to\infty$, $p_{\max}\le\bar p_i$ for $i$ large, so the truncation is inactive. Hence, almost surely, $E_{i-1}$ holds for all $i$ beyond a finite random time.

\emph{Step 2: Robbins--Siegmund.} Let $V_i=\|\delta_i\|^2$. Since $\Pi_\Theta$ is non-expansive and $\beta^*=\Pi_\Theta(\beta^*)$,
\[
V_i\le\|\delta_{i-1}-\gamma_iP_{i-1}g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\|^2=V_{i-1}-2\gamma_i\langle\delta_{i-1},P_{i-1}g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\rangle+\gamma_i^2\|P_{i-1}g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\|^2 .
\]
The variables $\delta_{i-1}$, $\beta_{i-1}$ and $P_{i-1}$ are $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable, and $X_i$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=m(\beta_{i-1})$ and $\mathbb{E}[\|g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\le\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]$. By construction $P_{i-1}$ is either $\hat P$ with $\|\hat P\|\le\bar p_i$ or zero, so $\|P_{i-1}\|\le\bar p_i$. Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}[V_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\le V_{i-1}-2\gamma_i\langle\delta_{i-1},P_{i-1}m(\beta_{i-1})\rangle+\gamma_i^2\bar p_i^2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2].
\]
On $E_{i-1}$, the inner product is at least $cV_{i-1}$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:mono}. On its complement it is at least $-\bar p_iK_0$, with $K_0=D_\Theta\sup_\Theta\|m\|\le D_\Theta\mathbb{E} B(X)$. Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}[V_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\le V_{i-1}-\underbrace{2c\gamma_iV_{i-1}\mathbf 1_{E_{i-1}}}_{c_{i-1}}+\underbrace{2\gamma_i\bar p_iK_0\mathbf 1_{E_{i-1}^c}+\gamma_i^2\bar p_i^2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]}_{b_{i-1}} .
\]
Both $b_{i-1}$ and $c_{i-1}$ are non-negative and $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable. The first part of $b_{i-1}$ vanishes for all $i$ large by Step~1. The second is deterministic and summable, because $\gamma_i^2\bar p_i^2\le Ci^{-2a+2\nu}$ and $2a-2\nu>1$. By (T1), $V_i$ converges almost surely to a finite limit $V_\infty$, and $\sum_i\gamma_iV_{i-1}\mathbf 1_{E_{i-1}}<\infty$. On the event $\{V_\infty>0\}$ we would have $V_{i-1}\mathbf 1_{E_{i-1}}\ge V_\infty/2$ for all $i$ large, which contradicts $\sum_i\gamma_i=\infty$. Hence $V_\infty=0$ almost surely, that is, $\beta_i\to\beta^*$, and $\bar\beta_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\beta_i\to\beta^*$ by Ces\`aro's lemma.

\emph{Step 3: limits of the preconditioner and of the projection.} Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}(c) gives the limits of $\Phi_n$, $W_n$, $H_n$ and $P(\Phi_n,W_n)$, and $P_n=P(\Phi_n,W_n)$ for $n$ large by Step~1. For the projection, let $r>0$ with $\bar B(\beta^*,2r)\subseteq\Theta$. By (T5), $B(X_i)\le i^{1/\kappa}$ for all $i$ large. On $E_{i-1}$,
\[
\gamma_i\|P_{i-1}g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})\|\le\gamma_0p_{\max}i^{-a+1/\kappa}\to0,
\]
because $a>1/2\ge2/\kappa>1/\kappa$. Since also $\|\delta_{i-1}\|\to0$, the point $\beta_{i-1}-\gamma_iP_{i-1}g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})$ lies in $\bar B(\beta^*,2r)\subseteq\Theta$ for all $i$ large, and the projection is inactive.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\varepsilon>(1-a)/\kappa$; without loss of generality $\varepsilon<a/2$, which is possible because $(1-a)/\kappa\le(1-a)/4<a/2$. Let $v_i=i^{-a/2+\varepsilon}$. Let $\iota$ be a finite random time after which the truncation and the projection are inactive and $E_{i-1}$ holds (Theorem~\ref{thm:as}). Let $e_i=g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})-m(\beta_{i-1})$. It is a martingale difference with $\mathbb{E}[\|e_i\|^\kappa\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\le2^\kappa\mathbb{E}[B(X)^\kappa]$. With $\tilde G$ as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:local}, $m(\beta_{i-1})=\tilde G(\beta_{i-1})\delta_{i-1}$; the representation used there only requires the segment from $\beta^*$ to $\beta_{i-1}$ to lie in the convex set $\Theta$. For $i>\iota$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linrec}
\delta_i=(I-\gamma_iA_{i-1})\delta_{i-1}-\gamma_iP_{i-1}e_i,\qquad A_{i-1}=P_{i-1}\tilde G(\beta_{i-1}).
\end{equation}
Since $\beta_{i-1}\to\beta^*$, $\tilde G(\beta_{i-1})\to G^*$ by continuity of $\bar G$. With $P_{i-1}\to P^*$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:as}), this gives $A_{i-1}\to P^*G^*=I$ almost surely.

\emph{Step 1: a scalar-weighted martingale.} Let $\tilde P_{i-1}=P_{i-1}\mathbf 1\{\|P_{i-1}\|\le p_{\max}\}$, which is $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable and bounded. Then $\xi_i=\tilde P_{i-1}e_i$ is a martingale difference with $\mathbb{E}\|\xi_i\|^\kappa\le c_\kappa:=p_{\max}^\kappa2^\kappa\mathbb{E}[B(X)^\kappa]$. With $i_1$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:weights}, define $Z_{i_1}=0$ and $Z_i=(1-\gamma_i)Z_{i-1}-\gamma_i\xi_i$ for $i>i_1$. Dividing by $\Gamma_{i_1,i}=(1-\gamma_i)\Gamma_{i_1,i-1}$ and summing, we get $Z_i=-\Gamma_{i_1,i}M_i$ with
\[
M_i=\sum_{k=i_1+1}^i\frac{\gamma_k}{\Gamma_{i_1,k}}\xi_k ,
\]
a martingale with deterministic weights.

Define block endpoints $t_0=i_1$ and $t_{k+1}=\min\{t>t_k:\sum_{j=t_k+1}^t\gamma_j\ge1\}$; they are finite because $\sum_j\gamma_j=\infty$. Since $\gamma_j\le1/2$, each block satisfies $1\le\sum_{j=t_k+1}^{t_{k+1}}\gamma_j<3/2$. Consequently $k\le\sum_{j\le t_k}\gamma_j\le Ct_k^{1-a}$.

By (T3) with $p=\kappa$, in the maximal form, and since $\Gamma_{i_1,t}=\Gamma_{i_1,j}\Gamma_{j,t}$ for $i_1\le j\le t$, Lemma~\ref{lem:weights} gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\max_{l\le t}\|M_l\|^\kappa\le Cc_\kappa\Big(\sum_{j=i_1+1}^t\frac{\gamma_j^2}{\Gamma_{i_1,j}^2}\Big)^{\kappa/2}=C\,\Gamma_{i_1,t}^{-\kappa}\Big(\sum_{j=i_1+1}^t\gamma_j^2\Gamma_{j,t}^2\Big)^{\kappa/2}\le C\,\Gamma_{i_1,t}^{-\kappa}\gamma_t^{\kappa/2}.
\]
For $t_k<i\le t_{k+1}$, $\Gamma_{i_1,i}\le\Gamma_{i_1,t_k}$, so $\|Z_i\|\le\Gamma_{i_1,t_k}\max_{l\le t_{k+1}}\|M_l\|$. Since $1-x\ge e^{-x-x^2}$ for $x\in[0,1/2]$, and $\sum_{j=t_k+1}^{t_{k+1}}\gamma_j^2\le\frac12\sum_{j=t_k+1}^{t_{k+1}}\gamma_j<3/4$, we have $\Gamma_{t_k,t_{k+1}}\ge e^{-3/2-3/4}=e^{-9/4}$. Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}\max_{t_k<i\le t_{k+1}}\|Z_i\|^\kappa\le C\Big(\frac{\Gamma_{i_1,t_k}}{\Gamma_{i_1,t_{k+1}}}\Big)^\kappa\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{\kappa/2}=C\,\Gamma_{t_k,t_{k+1}}^{-\kappa}\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{\kappa/2}\le C\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{\kappa/2}.
\]
Choose $\theta>0$ with $(1+\theta)(1-a)/\kappa<\varepsilon$. By Markov's inequality,
\[
\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{t_k<i\le t_{k+1}}\|Z_i\|>k^{(1+\theta)/\kappa}\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{1/2}\Big)\le\frac{C\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{\kappa/2}}{k^{1+\theta}\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{\kappa/2}}=Ck^{-1-\theta},
\]
which is summable in $k$. By Borel--Cantelli, almost surely, for all large $k$ and all $t_k<i\le t_{k+1}$,
\[
\|Z_i\|\le k^{(1+\theta)/\kappa}\gamma_{t_{k+1}}^{1/2}\le Ci^{(1+\theta)(1-a)/\kappa}\gamma_i^{1/2}\le Cv_i,
\]
where we used $k\le Ct_k^{1-a}\le Ci^{1-a}$ and $\gamma_{t_{k+1}}\le\gamma_i$. Hence $\|Z_i\|=O(v_i)$ almost surely.

\emph{Step 2: comparison.} Let $\iota'\ge\max(\iota,i_1)$ be a finite random time after which $\|P_{i-1}\|\le p_{\max}$, so that $\xi_i=P_{i-1}e_i$, and $\|A_{i-1}-I\|\le1/2$. For $i>\iota'$, \eqref{eq:linrec} and the definition of $Z_i$ give for $\Delta_i=\delta_i-Z_i$
\[
\Delta_i=(I-\gamma_iA_{i-1})\delta_{i-1}-(1-\gamma_i)Z_{i-1}=(I-\gamma_iA_{i-1})\Delta_{i-1}-\gamma_i(A_{i-1}-I)Z_{i-1}.
\]
Since $I-\gamma_iA_{i-1}=(1-\gamma_i)I-\gamma_i(A_{i-1}-I)$, we have $\|I-\gamma_iA_{i-1}\|\le1-\gamma_i/2$. Hence
\[
\|\Delta_i\|\le(1-\gamma_i/2)\|\Delta_{i-1}\|+\gamma_i\eta_iv_{i-1},\qquad\eta_i=\frac{\|A_{i-1}-I\|\,\|Z_{i-1}\|}{v_{i-1}}\to0 .
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:det} with $q=a/2-\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ gives $\|\Delta_i\|=o(v_i)$, hence $\|\delta_i\|=O(v_i)$. For the average, $\|\bar\beta_n-\beta^*\|\le n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\|\delta_i\|\le C(\omega)n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}i^{-q}\le C(\omega)v_n/(1-q)$.

\emph{Step 3: Jacobian and weights.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}(b) with $\varepsilon'<\varepsilon$ and the Lipschitz continuity of $\bar G$,
\[
\|\Phi_i-G^*\|\le\frac{\bar L}i\sum_{j\le i}\|\bar\beta_{j-1}-\beta^*\|+O\big(i^{-1/2+\varepsilon'}\big)=O(v_i),
\]
because $i^{-1}\sum_{j\le i}v_j=O(v_i)$ and $-1/2+\varepsilon'<-a/2+\varepsilon$. The same argument applies to $S_i-\Omega^*$, using the Lipschitz continuity of $\Omega$. Finally, $\|W_i-\Omega^{*-1}\|=\|W_i(\Omega^*-S_i)\Omega^{*-1}\|\le\|W_i\|\,\|S_i-\Omega^*\|\,\|\Omega^{*-1}\|$, and $\|W_i\|\le2/\lambda_0$ for $i$ large.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\kappa>\kappa(a)$, we have $(1-a)/\kappa<(1-a)/2$ and $(1-a)/\kappa<(2a-1)/4$. We can therefore fix $\varepsilon$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eps}
\frac{1-a}\kappa<\varepsilon<\min\Big\{\frac{1-a}2,\ \frac{2a-1}4\Big\},
\end{equation}
and Theorem~\ref{thm:rate} applies with $v_i=i^{-a/2+\varepsilon}$. Let $\iota$ be as in the previous proof. For $i>\iota$, \eqref{eq:linrec} gives $\delta_i=\delta_{i-1}-\gamma_iP_{i-1}m(\beta_{i-1})-\gamma_iP_{i-1}e_i$, which can be rearranged as
\[
\delta_{i-1}=\frac{\delta_{i-1}-\delta_i}{\gamma_i}-P_{i-1}e_i-\rho_{i-1},\qquad\rho_{i-1}=P_{i-1}m(\beta_{i-1})-\delta_{i-1}.
\]
Write $e_i=\xi^0_i+\zeta_i$, where $\xi^0_i=g(X_i,\beta^*)$ are i.i.d.\ with mean $m(\beta^*)=0$ and covariance $\Omega^*$, and
\[
\zeta_i=g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})-g(X_i,\beta^*)-m(\beta_{i-1}).
\]
The $\zeta_i$ are martingale differences, and since $\|g(x,\beta)-g(x,\beta^*)\|\le B(x)\|\beta-\beta^*\|$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta_i\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\le\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\,\|\delta_{i-1}\|^2 .
\]
Using $P_{i-1}e_i=P^*\xi^0_i+P^*\zeta_i+(P_{i-1}-P^*)e_i$, we obtain for $\iota<k\le n$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decomp}
\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k\delta_{i-1}=-P^*\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k\xi_i^0+R^{(1)}_k-R^{(2)}_k-R^{(3)}_k-R^{(4)}_k,
\end{equation}
where
\[
\textstyle R^{(1)}_k=\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k\frac{\delta_{i-1}-\delta_i}{\gamma_i},\quad R^{(2)}_k=P^*\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k\zeta_i,\quad R^{(3)}_k=\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k(P_{i-1}-P^*)e_i,\quad R^{(4)}_k=\sum_{i=\iota+1}^k\rho_{i-1}.
\]
Here $\iota$ is a random time, finite almost surely but not a stopping time. We show that $n^{-1/2}\max_{\iota<k\le n}\|R^{(l)}_k\|\to0$ in probability for $l=1,\dots,4$. The terms with $i\le\iota$ are finitely many and do not depend on $n$: $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\le\iota}\|\delta_{i-1}\|\le n^{-1/2}\iota D_\Theta\to0$ and $n^{-1/2}\|P^*\sum_{i\le\iota}\xi^0_i\|\to0$ almost surely. Let $\iota'\ge\iota$ be as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rate}.

\emph{$R^{(1)}$.} By Abel summation,
\[
R^{(1)}_k=\frac{\delta_\iota}{\gamma_{\iota+1}}-\frac{\delta_k}{\gamma_k}+\sum_{i=\iota+1}^{k-1}\delta_i\Big(\frac1{\gamma_{i+1}}-\frac1{\gamma_i}\Big),
\]
and $0\le1/\gamma_{i+1}-1/\gamma_i=\gamma_0^{-1}\big((i+1+i_0)^a-(i+i_0)^a\big)\le a\gamma_0^{-1}(i+i_0)^{a-1}$. With $\|\delta_i\|\le C(\omega)v_i$ for all $i$,
\[
\max_{\iota<k\le n}\|R^{(1)}_k\|\le C(\omega)\Big(1+\max_{k\le n}k^av_k+\sum_{i\le n}i^{a-1}v_i\Big)\le C(\omega)\big(1+n^{a/2+\varepsilon}\big),
\]
and $n^{a/2+\varepsilon-1/2}\to0$ by \eqref{eq:eps}.

\emph{$R^{(4)}$.} Since $\|G(x,\beta)-G(x,\beta')\|\le L(x)\|\beta-\beta'\|$, the argument for $\tilde G$ gives $\|m(\beta)-G^*(\beta-\beta^*)\|\le\bar L\|\beta-\beta^*\|^2/2$. Using also $P_{i-1}\Phi_{i-1}=I$, for $i>\iota$
\[
\begin{aligned}\|\rho_{i-1}\|&=\big\|P_{i-1}\big(m(\beta_{i-1})-G^*\delta_{i-1}\big)+P_{i-1}(G^*-\Phi_{i-1})\delta_{i-1}\big\|\\&\le p_{\max}\big(\bar L\|\delta_{i-1}\|^2/2+\|\Phi_{i-1}-G^*\|\,\|\delta_{i-1}\|\big)\le C(\omega)v_{i-1}^2\end{aligned}
\]
by Theorem~\ref{thm:rate}. Thus $\max_{k\le n}\|R^{(4)}_k\|\le C(\omega)\sum_{i\le n}i^{-a+2\varepsilon}\le C(\omega)n^{1-a+2\varepsilon}$, where $a-2\varepsilon<1$. Moreover $n^{1/2-a+2\varepsilon}\to0$ by \eqref{eq:eps}.

\emph{$R^{(2)}$.} Since $\iota$ is not a stopping time, we compare with $M^{(2)}_k=P^*\sum_{i=1}^k\zeta_i$, a martingale for $(\mathcal{F}_k)$. Since $R^{(2)}_k=M^{(2)}_k-M^{(2)}_{\iota\wedge k}$, we have $\max_{k\le n}\|R^{(2)}_k\|\le2\max_{k\le n}\|M^{(2)}_k\|$. Its predictable quadratic variation satisfies
\[
\operatorname{tr}\langle M^{(2)}\rangle_n\le\|P^*\|^2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\sum_{i\le n}\|\delta_{i-1}\|^2,
\]
and $n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\|\delta_{i-1}\|^2\to0$ almost surely by Theorem~\ref{thm:as} and Ces\`aro's lemma. By (T4) applied to $n^{-1/2}M^{(2)}$, $n^{-1/2}\max_{k\le n}\|R^{(2)}_k\|\to0$ in probability.

\emph{$R^{(3)}$.} Let $M^{(3)}_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(\tilde P_{i-1}-P^*)e_i$, with $\tilde P_{i-1}$ the bounded predictable matrix of the previous proof. It is a martingale with
\[
\operatorname{tr}\langle M^{(3)}\rangle_n\le4\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\sum_{i\le n}\|\tilde P_{i-1}-P^*\|^2,
\]
and $n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\|\tilde P_{i-1}-P^*\|^2\to0$ almost surely, because $\tilde P_{i-1}=P_{i-1}\to P^*$. By (T4), $n^{-1/2}\max_{k\le n}\|M^{(3)}_k\|\to0$ in probability. Since $\tilde P_{i-1}=P_{i-1}$ for $i>\iota'$, $R^{(3)}_k$ differs from $M^{(3)}_k-M^{(3)}_{\iota'\wedge k}$ by a sum of finitely many terms that does not depend on $n$, and the claim follows.

\emph{Conclusion.} Since $\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor nt\rfloor}(\beta_i-\beta^*)=\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor nt\rfloor}\delta_{i-1}+\delta_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}-\delta_0$ and $\max_k\|\delta_k\|\le D_\Theta$, \eqref{eq:decomp} and the bounds above give \eqref{eq:bahadur}. By Donsker's theorem \cite[Theorem~14.1]{Billingsley1999}, applied to $\lambda^{\top}\xi^0_i$ for each $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{d_g}$, together with the Cram\'er--Wold device for the finite-dimensional distributions and the fact that a vector of tight coordinate processes with continuous limits is tight, we have $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\le\lfloor nt\rfloor}\xi^0_i\Rightarrow\Omega^{*1/2}\mathbf B_g$ in $D[0,1]^{d_g}$, with $\mathbf B_g$ a standard $d_g$-dimensional Brownian motion. Moreover
\[
P^*\Omega^*P^{*\top}=\Sigma^*G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}\Omega^*\Omega^{*-1}G^*\Sigma^*=\Sigma^* .
\]
Since the limit has continuous paths, \eqref{eq:bahadur} and Slutsky's lemma give $\mathbb B_n\Rightarrow-P^*\Omega^{*1/2}\mathbf B_g$, a Gaussian process with the law of $\Sigma^{*1/2}\mathbf B$. Finally, $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*)=\mathbb B_n(1)$.

(a) By Theorem~\ref{thm:as}, $H_{n,kk}\to\Sigma^*_{kk}>0$ almost surely. By Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt} at $t=1$, $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_{n,k}-\beta^*_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\Sigma^*_{kk})$. Slutsky's lemma gives $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_{n,k}-\beta^*_k)/H_{n,kk}^{1/2}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$, so the coverage probability converges to $\mathbb{P}(|N(0,1)|\le z_{1-\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$.

(b) Since $s(\bar\beta_s-\beta^*)=\sqrt n\,\mathbb B_n(s/n)$, we have $s(\bar\beta_s-\bar\beta_n)=\sqrt n\big(\mathbb B_n(s/n)-\frac sn\mathbb B_n(1)\big)$ and
\[
V_n=\frac1n\sum_{s=1}^n\Big(\mathbb B_n(\tfrac sn)-\tfrac sn\mathbb B_n(1)\Big)\Big(\mathbb B_n(\tfrac sn)-\tfrac sn\mathbb B_n(1)\Big)^{\top} .
\]
Consider the map $\Psi$ from $D[0,1]^{d_\beta}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d_\beta}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_\beta\timesd_\beta}$ that sends $f$ to $\big(f(1),\int_0^1(f(r)-rf(1))(f(r)-rf(1))^{\top}\,\mathrm{d} r\big)$. Convergence in the Skorokhod topology to a continuous function is uniform convergence, and $\Psi$ is continuous for the uniform norm. Hence $\Psi$ is continuous at every continuous $f$.

The process $\mathbb B_n$ is constant on each interval $[(s-1)/n,s/n)$, and $\|\mathbb B_n(s/n)-\mathbb B_n((s-1)/n)\|=n^{-1/2}\|\delta_s\|\le n^{-1/2}D_\Theta$. Also $|r-s/n|\le1/n$ on that interval. Hence each summand of $V_n$ differs from the integral of the corresponding integrand over $[(s-1)/n,s/n)$ by at most $Cn^{-1}\cdot n^{-1/2}\big(1+\sup_t\|\mathbb B_n(t)\|\big)^2$. The Riemann sum $V_n$ therefore differs from the second component of $\Psi(\mathbb B_n)$ by at most $Cn^{-1/2}\big(1+\sup_t\|\mathbb B_n(t)\|\big)^2$, which tends to zero in probability because $\sup_t\|\mathbb B_n(t)\|$ is tight. By Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt} and the continuous mapping theorem,
\[
\big(\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*),V_n\big)\Rightarrow\Big(\Sigma^{*1/2}\mathbf B(1),\ \Sigma^{*1/2}\int_0^1(\mathbf B(r)-r\mathbf B(1))(\mathbf B(r)-r\mathbf B(1))^{\top}\,\mathrm{d} r\,\Sigma^{*1/2}\Big).
\]
The $k$th coordinate of $\Sigma^{*1/2}\mathbf B$ is $(\Sigma^*_{kk})^{1/2}$ times a standard Brownian motion $\mathbf b$, and the $(k,k)$ entry of the second component is $\Sigma^*_{kk}\int_0^1(\mathbf b(r)-r\mathbf b(1))^2\,\mathrm{d} r$. The factor $\Sigma^*_{kk}$ cancels in the ratio. The denominator of the limit is almost surely positive, because a Brownian bridge is not identically zero. The continuous mapping theorem for the ratio gives the stated limit.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varepsilon$ be as in \eqref{eq:eps} and $v_i=i^{-a/2+\varepsilon}$.

\emph{Step 1: linearization error.} For $b,b'\in\Theta$, Taylor's formula with integral remainder and the Lipschitz bound on $G$ give
\[
\big\|g(x,b)-g(x,b')-G(x,b')(b-b')\big\|=\Big\|\int_0^1\big(G(x,b'+t(b-b'))-G(x,b')\big)\,\mathrm{d} t\,(b-b')\Big\|\le\tfrac12L(x)\|b-b'\|^2 .
\]
With $b=\bar\beta_n$, $b'=\bar\beta_{i-1}$ and $\|b-b'\|^2\le2\|\bar\beta_n-\beta^*\|^2+2\|\bar\beta_{i-1}-\beta^*\|^2$, summing over $i\le n$ gives
\[
\sqrt n\|\hat g_n-\bar g_n(\bar\beta_n)\|\le\sqrt n\,\|\bar\beta_n-\beta^*\|^2\,\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}L(X_i)+\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}L(X_i)\|\bar\beta_{i-1}-\beta^*\|^2 .
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:rate} and the strong law of large numbers for $L(X_i)$, the first term is $O(n^{1/2}v_n^2)=O(n^{1/2-a+2\varepsilon})$. For the second, $\|\bar\beta_{i-1}-\beta^*\|^2\le C(\omega)i^{-a+2\varepsilon}$ for $i\ge1$. Moreover $T_i=\sum_{j\le i}L(X_j)\le C(\omega)i$ by the strong law, and $q=a-2\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ by \eqref{eq:eps}. By (T6), $\sum_{i\le n}L(X_i)i^{-a+2\varepsilon}\le C(\omega)n^{1-a+2\varepsilon}$, so the second term is also $O(n^{1/2-a+2\varepsilon})$. Both tend to zero by \eqref{eq:eps}, because $1/2-a+2\varepsilon<0$ is equivalent to $\varepsilon<(2a-1)/4$. This proves the first claim.

\emph{Step 2: limit.} By the integral form of the mean value theorem,
\[
\bar g_n(\bar\beta_n)=\bar g_n(\beta^*)+\check G_n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*),\qquad\check G_n=\int_0^1\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}G\big(X_i,\beta^*+t(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*)\big)\,\mathrm{d} t,
\]
and $\|\check G_n-G^*\|\le\|\bar\beta_n-\beta^*\|\,n^{-1}\sum_iL(X_i)+\|n^{-1}\sum_iG(X_i,\beta^*)-G^*\|\to0$ almost surely by the strong law. By \eqref{eq:bahadur} at $t=1$, $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*)=-P^*\sqrt n\,\bar g_n(\beta^*)+o_P(1)$, and $\sqrt n\,\bar g_n(\beta^*)\Rightarrow N(0,\Omega^*)$ by the central limit theorem. Combining these with Step~1,
\[
\sqrt n\,\hat g_n=\big(I-G^*P^*\big)\sqrt n\,\bar g_n(\beta^*)+(\check G_n-G^*)\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n-\beta^*)+o_P(1)\Rightarrow(I-G^*P^*)\Omega^{*1/2}\mathcal Z,
\]
with $\mathcal Z\sim N(0,I_{d_g})$. Let $Q=\Omega^{*-1/2}G^*\Sigma^*G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1/2}$. It is symmetric and idempotent, so it is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $\Omega^{*-1/2}G^*$, which has dimension $d_\beta$. Since $P^*=\Sigma^*G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}$,
\[
\Omega^{*-1/2}(I-G^*P^*)\Omega^{*1/2}=I-Q .
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:as}, $H_n$ exists for $n$ large and
\[
W_n-W_n\Phi_nH_n\Phi_n^{\top} W_n\to\Omega^{*-1}-\Omega^{*-1}G^*\Sigma^*G^{*\top}\Omega^{*-1}=\Omega^{*-1/2}(I-Q)\Omega^{*-1/2}
\]
almost surely. By the continuous mapping theorem,
\[
\mathcal J_n\Rightarrow\mathcal Z^{\top}(I-Q)\Omega^{*1/2}\,\Omega^{*-1/2}(I-Q)\Omega^{*-1/2}\,\Omega^{*1/2}(I-Q)\mathcal Z=\|(I-Q)\mathcal Z\|^2\sim\chi^2_{d_g-d_\beta},
\]
since $I-Q$ is an orthogonal projection of rank $d_g-d_\beta$. Replacing the projected weight by $W_n\to\Omega^{*-1}$ gives the limit $\mathcal Z^{\top}(I-Q)(I-Q)\mathcal Z$, which is the same. Hence the unprojected statistic $n\hat g_n^{\top} W_n\hat g_n$ has the same limit.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $j\ge1$, $\xi_{r+jk}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{r+jk}$-measurable, and $\mathbb{E}[\xi_{r+jk}\mid\mathcal{F}_{r+(j-1)k}]=0$ because $r+(j-1)k=(r+jk)-k$ and $r+jk>k$. Write $\sum_{i\le l}w_i\xi_i=\sum_{i\le k\wedge l}w_i\xi_i+\sum_{r=1}^kM^{(r)}_l$ with $M^{(r)}_l=\sum_{j\ge1:\,r+jk\le l}w_{r+jk}\xi_{r+jk}$. Each $M^{(r)}$ is a martingale in the index $j$.

(a) Take $w_i=1$. By (T2), each $M^{(r)}$, which has at most $n/k$ terms up to $n$, is $O(n^{1/2+\varepsilon'})$, and the first $k$ terms are a fixed finite sum.

(b) Since $(\sum_{r=0}^ka_r)^p\le(k+1)^{p-1}\sum_ra_r^p$, it suffices to bound each part. For the martingales, (T3) in its maximal form and \eqref{eq:burkholder} give $\mathbb{E}\max_{l\le t}\|M^{(r)}_l\|^p\le C_{p,d}c_p\big(\sum_{i\le t}w_i^2\big)^{p/2}$. For the first $k$ terms, H\"older's inequality gives $\mathbb{E}\max_{l\le k}\|\sum_{i\le l}w_i\xi_i\|^p\le k^{p-1}\sum_{i\le k}|w_i|^p\mathbb{E}\|\xi_i\|^p\le k^{p-1}c_p\big(\sum_iw_i^2\big)^{p/2}$.

(c) Each $M^{(r)}$ is a martingale with $\sup_l\mathbb{E}\|M^{(r)}_l\|^2\le c_p^{2/p}\sum_iw_i^2<\infty$, and therefore converges almost surely by the martingale convergence theorem.

(d) The predictable quadratic variation of $M^{(r)}$ (with $w_i=1$) up to time $n$ is at most $\sum_{i\le n}\vartheta_{i-k}$. By (T4) applied to $n^{-1/2}M^{(r)}$, $n^{-1/2}\max_{l\le n}\|M^{(r)}_l\|\to0$ in probability for each $r$. The first $k$ terms are negligible.

label: lem:precondLR
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Jacobian and long-run weights

title: Proof
body_md:
We first note that $\Omega_{\rm LR}$ is Lipschitz on $\Theta$. Indeed, for each $|h|\le L$,
\[
\big\|\mathbb{E}[g(X_0,\beta)g(X_h,\beta)^{\top}]-\mathbb{E}[g(X_0,\beta')g(X_h,\beta')^{\top}]\big\|\le2\mathbb{E}[B(X_0)B(X_h)]\|\beta-\beta'\|\le2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\|\beta-\beta'\|,
\]
so $\Omega_{\rm LR}$ is Lipschitz with constant $2(2L+1)\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]$. Also $\bar G$ is Lipschitz with constant $\bar L$.

(b), Jacobian. As in Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}, $\Phi_i=(n_0+i)^{-1}\big(n_0\Phi_0+\sum_{j\le i}G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})\big)$. For $j>D$ write
\[
\begin{aligned}G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})-\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})&=\underbrace{G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-D})-\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-D})}_{\Delta^\Phi_j}\\&\quad+\underbrace{G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-1})-G(X_j,\bar\beta_{j-D})}_{\text{norm}\le L(X_j)\|\bar\beta_{j-1}-\bar\beta_{j-D}\|}\\&\quad-\underbrace{\big(\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-1})-\bar G(\bar\beta_{j-D})\big)}_{\text{norm}\le\bar L\|\bar\beta_{j-1}-\bar\beta_{j-D}\|}.
.\end{aligned}
\]
By (D1), $\mathbb{E}[\Delta^\Phi_j\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-D}]=0$, and $\mathbb{E}\|\Delta_j^\Phi\|^2\le4\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]$. Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(a) with delay $k=D$ gives $\sum_{j\le i}\Delta^\Phi_j=O(i^{1/2+\varepsilon'})$. By \eqref{eq:barstep}, $\|\bar\beta_{j-1}-\bar\beta_{j-D}\|\le D_\Theta\sum_{l=j-D+1}^{j-1}l^{-1}\le2D\,D_\Theta/j$ for $j\ge2D$. By (T6) and (D2), $\sum_{j\le i}(L(X_j)+\bar L)/j\le C(\omega)(2+\log i)$. Dividing by $n_0+i$ gives the bound for $\Phi_i$, since $\log i/i=O(i^{-1/2})$ and the terms with $j\le2D$ and the pilot term are $O(1/i)$.

(b), weights. From \eqref{eq:lrv}, $S_i=(n_0+i)^{-1}\big(n_0S_0+\sum_{j\le i}y_j\big)$. For $j>K$ let $b_j=\bar\beta_{j-K}$, which is $\mathcal{F}_{j-K}$-measurable, and let $\tilde y_j$ be $y_j$ with every $s_{j-h}=g(X_{j-h},\bar\beta_{j-h-1})$, $0\le h\le L$, replaced by $\tilde s_{j-h}=g(X_{j-h},b_j)$. By (D1) and stationarity,
\[
\begin{aligned}\mathbb{E}[\tilde y_j\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-K}]&=\Big(\mathbb{E}[g(X_0,\beta)g(X_0,\beta)^{\top}]\\&\qquad+\sum_{h=1}^L\big(\mathbb{E}[g(X_h,\beta)g(X_0,\beta)^{\top}]+\mathbb{E}[g(X_0,\beta)g(X_h,\beta)^{\top}]\big)\Big)\Big|_{\beta=b_j}=\Omega_{\rm LR}(b_j).\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover $\|\tilde y_j\|\le(2L+1)\big(\sum_{h=0}^LB(X_{j-h})\big)^2$, so $\mathbb{E}\|\tilde y_j-\Omega_{\rm LR}(b_j)\|^2\le C\mathbb{E}[B(X)^4]$. Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(a) with delay $k=K$ gives $\sum_{j\le i}\big(\tilde y_j-\Omega_{\rm LR}(b_j)\big)=O(i^{1/2+\varepsilon'})$.

Next, the indices $j-h-1$ for $0\le h\le L$ lie between $j-K$ and $j-1$. So by \eqref{eq:barstep}, $\|\bar\beta_{j-h-1}-b_j\|\le2K\,D_\Theta/j$ for $j\ge2K$. Hence $\|s_{j-h}-\tilde s_{j-h}\|\le2K\,D_\Theta B(X_{j-h})/j$. Since $y_j$ is a sum of $2L+1$ products $ab^{\top}$ with $\|ab^{\top}-\tilde a\tilde b^{\top}\|\le\|a-\tilde a\|\,\|b\|+\|\tilde a\|\,\|b-\tilde b\|$,
\[
\|y_j-\tilde y_j\|\le\frac Cj\sum_{h=0}^LB(X_{j-h})^2\le C\sum_{h=0}^L\frac{B(X_{j-h})^2}{j-h},
\]
and $\sum_{j\le i}\|y_j-\tilde y_j\|\le C(\omega)(2+\log i)$ by (T6) and (D2) applied to $B(X)^2$. Finally, $\|\Omega_{\rm LR}(b_j)-\Omega_{\rm LR}(\bar\beta_{j-1})\|\le C\|\bar\beta_{j-K}-\bar\beta_{j-1}\|\le C/j$. Collecting terms, together with the finitely many terms with $j\le2K$, which involve the pilot values $s_j$, $j\le0$, and contribute $O(1/i)$, proves the bound for $S_i$.

(a) and (c) follow from (b) exactly as in Lemma~\ref{lem:precond}. The eigenvalues of $\Omega_{\rm LR}(\beta)$ lie in $[\lambda_0,\Lambda]$ by definition, and $\Omega_{\rm LR}$ and $\bar G$ are continuous. Once $S_i$ is positive definite, $W_i=S_i^{-1}$ by the definition of the weights.

(d) By (a), there is a finite random index after which $\Phi_{i-1}\in\mathcal N$, $\|S_{i-1}\|\le2\Lambda$ and $W_{i-1},W_i\in\mathcal W$. By (T5) and (D2), also $B(X_l)\le l^{1/\kappa}$ for $l\ge i-L$. Then
\begin{gather*}
\|\Phi_i-\Phi_{i-1}\|=\frac{\|G(X_i,\bar\beta_{i-1})-\Phi_{i-1}\|}{n_0+i}\le\frac{i^{1/\kappa}+\phi_{\max}}{i},\\ \|S_i-S_{i-1}\|=\frac{\|y_i-S_{i-1}\|}{n_0+i}\le\frac{(2L+1)^3i^{2/\kappa}+2\Lambda}{i},
\end{gather*}
and $\|W_i-W_{i-1}\|=\|W_i(S_{i-1}-S_i)W_{i-1}\|\le4\lambda_0^{-2}\|S_i-S_{i-1}\|$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: eventual regime and decomposition.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:precondLR}(a), \eqref{eq:Pbound}, $\bar p_i\to\infty$ and (T5), there is a finite random index $\iota_0$ such that for all $i\ge\iota_0$: $\Phi_i\in\mathcal N$, $W_i\in\mathcal W$, the truncation is inactive, $P_i=P(\Phi_i,W_i)$, $\|P_i\|\le p_{\max}$, $B(X_i)\le i^{1/\kappa}$, and the bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:precondLR}(d) holds.

For $i\ge\iota_0+D$, all indices $i-D,\dots,i-1$ belong to this regime. Write $g_i=g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})$ and
\[
e_i=g(X_i,\beta_{i-D})-m(\beta_{i-D}),\qquad r_i=P_{i-D}\big(g(X_i,\beta_{i-1})-g(X_i,\beta_{i-D})\big)+(P_{i-1}-P_{i-D})g_i ,
\]
so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delaydec}
P_{i-1}g_i=P_{i-D}m(\beta_{i-D})+P_{i-D}e_i+r_i .
\end{equation}
By (D1), $\mathbb{E}[e_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[\|e_i\|^\kappa\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]\le2^\kappa\mathbb{E}[B(X)^\kappa]$. Since $\Pi_\Theta$ is non-expansive and $\beta_{l-1}\in\Theta$, $\|\beta_l-\beta_{l-1}\|\le\gamma_l\|P_{l-1}g(X_l,\beta_{l-1})\|\le p_{\max}\gamma_ll^{1/\kappa}$ in the regime. Since $\gamma_{i-L}/\gamma_i$ is bounded,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stepdiff}
\|\beta_{i-1}-\beta_{i-D}\|\le\sum_{l=i-D+1}^{i-1}p_{\max}\gamma_ll^{1/\kappa}\le C\gamma_ii^{1/\kappa}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:Plip} and Lemma~\ref{lem:precondLR}(d), $\|P_{i-1}-P_{i-D}\|\le C_P\sum_{l=i-D+1}^{i-1}\big(\|\Phi_l-\Phi_{l-1}\|+\|W_l-W_{l-1}\|\big)\le Ci^{2/\kappa-1}$. With $\|g(X_i,\beta)-g(X_i,\beta')\|\le B(X_i)\|\beta-\beta'\|$ and $\|g_i\|\le B(X_i)\le i^{1/\kappa}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rbound}
\|r_i\|\le C\big(\gamma_ii^{2/\kappa}+i^{3/\kappa-1}\big).
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 2: almost sure convergence.} Let $V_i=\|\delta_i\|^2$. For $i\ge\iota_0+D$, non-expansiveness of $\Pi_\Theta$ gives $V_i\le V_{i-1}-2\gamma_i\langle\delta_{i-1},P_{i-1}g_i\rangle+\gamma_i^2\|P_{i-1}g_i\|^2$. By \eqref{eq:delaydec},
\[
\langle\delta_{i-1},P_{i-1}g_i\rangle=\langle\delta_{i-D},P_{i-D}m(\beta_{i-D})\rangle+\chi_i+\langle\delta_{i-D},r_i\rangle+\langle\delta_{i-1}-\delta_{i-D},P_{i-1}g_i\rangle,\qquad\chi_i=\langle\delta_{i-D},P_{i-D}e_i\rangle .
\]
The first term is at least $cV_{i-D}$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:mono}. By \eqref{eq:stepdiff} and \eqref{eq:rbound}, the third and fourth terms are bounded in absolute value by $C(\gamma_ii^{2/\kappa}+i^{3/\kappa-1})$, and $\gamma_i^2\|P_{i-1}g_i\|^2\le p_{\max}^2\gamma_i^2i^{2/\kappa}$. Hence, for $i\ge\iota_0+D$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathRS}
V_i\le V_{i-1}-2c\gamma_iV_{i-D}-2\gamma_i\chi_i+b_i,\qquad b_i=C\big(\gamma_i^2i^{2/\kappa}+\gamma_ii^{3/\kappa-1}\big).
\end{equation}
The sequence $b_i$ is summable. First, $\gamma_i^2i^{2/\kappa}\le Ci^{-2a+2/\kappa}$ and $2a-2/\kappa>1$ because $\kappa>2/(2a-1)$. Second, $\gamma_ii^{3/\kappa-1}\le Ci^{-1-(a-3/\kappa)}$, and $a>3/\kappa$. To see the last inequality: if $a\le3/4$, then $2/(2a-1)\ge3/a$ (equivalent to $2a\ge6a-3$), so $\kappa>3/a$; if $a>3/4$, then $3/a<4\le\kappa$.

Let $\tilde\chi_i=\langle\delta_{i-D},\tilde P_{i-D}e_i\rangle$, with $\tilde P_{i-D}=P_{i-D}\mathbf 1\{\|P_{i-D}\|\le p_{\max}\}$. Then $\tilde\chi_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable, $\mathbb{E}[\tilde\chi_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}\tilde\chi_i^2\le4D_\Theta^2p_{\max}^2\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]$. Set $\tilde\chi_i=0$ for $i\le D$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(c) with delay $k=D$ and $w_i=\gamma_i$, $\sum_i\gamma_i\tilde\chi_i$ converges almost surely. Since $\tilde\chi_i=\chi_i$ for $i\ge\iota_0+D$, the series $\sum_{i\ge\iota_0+D}\gamma_i\chi_i$ converges.

Let $\tau_i=\sum_{j>i}\gamma_j\chi_j$ and $\bar b_i=\sum_{j>i}b_j$, both tending to zero, and let $U_i=V_i-2\tau_i+\bar b_i$. Since $\gamma_i\chi_i=\tau_{i-1}-\tau_i$ and $b_i=\bar b_{i-1}-\bar b_i$, \eqref{eq:pathRS} becomes
\[
U_i\le U_{i-1}-2c\gamma_iV_{i-D}\qquad(i\ge\iota_0+D).
\]
Thus $U_i$ is non-increasing and bounded below by $-2\sup_j|\tau_j|>-\infty$. Hence $U_i$ converges, and $\sum_i\gamma_iV_{i-D}<\infty$. Consequently $V_i=U_i+2\tau_i-\bar b_i$ converges. Since $\sum_i\gamma_i=\infty$, $\liminf_iV_{i-D}=0$, so $V_i\to0$. Thus $\beta_i\to\beta^*$ and $\bar\beta_i\to\beta^*$. Lemma~\ref{lem:precondLR}(c) gives the limits of $\Phi_n$, $W_n$, $H_n$ and $P_n$. The projection is eventually inactive by the argument of Step~3 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:as}, which uses only $B(X_i)\le i^{1/\kappa}$ and $a>1/\kappa$.

\emph{Step 3: rates.} Fix $\varepsilon>\max\{(1-a)/\kappa,\,2/\kappa-a/2,\,3/\kappa-1+a/2\}$. Without loss of generality $\varepsilon<a/2$. This is possible because each of the three lower bounds is smaller than $a/2$: $(1-a)/\kappa<a/2$ since $\kappa\ge4>2(1-a)/a$; $2/\kappa-a/2<a/2$ since $\kappa\ge4>2/a$; and $3/\kappa-1+a/2<a/2$ since $\kappa>3$.

Let $v_i=i^{-a/2+\varepsilon}$, and let $\iota_1\ge\iota_0+D$ be a finite random index after which the projection is inactive and $\|A_{i-D}-I\|\le1/2$, where $A_{i-D}=P_{i-D}\tilde G(\beta_{i-D})\to I$. For $i>\iota_1$, \eqref{eq:delaydec} and $P_{i-D}m(\beta_{i-D})=A_{i-D}\delta_{i-D}$ give
\[
\delta_i=(I-\gamma_iA_{i-D})\delta_{i-1}-\gamma_iP_{i-D}e_i+\gamma_if_i,\qquad f_i=A_{i-D}(\delta_{i-1}-\delta_{i-D})-r_i .
\]
By \eqref{eq:stepdiff} and \eqref{eq:rbound}, $\|f_i\|\le C(\gamma_ii^{2/\kappa}+i^{3/\kappa-1})$.

Enlarging $i_1$ if necessary (Lemma~\ref{lem:weights} holds for every larger $i_1$), we assume $i_1\ge D$. Define $Z_i$ as in Step~1 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rate}, with $\xi_i=\tilde P_{i-D}e_i$ for $i>D$ and $\xi_i=0$ for $i\le D$. These satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}\|\xi_i\|^\kappa\le p_{\max}^\kappa2^\kappa\mathbb{E}[B(X)^\kappa]$. Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(b) with delay $k=D$ replaces Doob's and Burkholder's inequalities in that step, so the bound $\mathbb{E}\max_{l\le t}\|M_l\|^\kappa\le C(\sum_{j\le t}\gamma_j^2/\Gamma_{i_1,j}^2)^{\kappa/2}$ still holds, and the rest of Step~1 is unchanged. Hence $\|Z_i\|=O(v_i)$. For $i>\iota_1$, $\Delta_i=\delta_i-Z_i$ satisfies
\[
\Delta_i=(I-\gamma_iA_{i-D})\Delta_{i-1}-\gamma_i(A_{i-D}-I)Z_{i-1}+\gamma_if_i ,
\]
hence $\|\Delta_i\|\le(1-\gamma_i/2)\|\Delta_{i-1}\|+\gamma_i\eta_iv_{i-1}$ with
\[
\eta_i=\frac{\|A_{i-D}-I\|\,\|Z_{i-1}\|+\|f_i\|}{v_{i-1}}\le o(1)+C\big(i^{-a/2+2/\kappa-\varepsilon}+i^{3/\kappa-1+a/2-\varepsilon}\big)\to0 ,
\]
by the choice of $\varepsilon$. Lemma~\ref{lem:det} gives $\|\Delta_i\|=o(v_i)$, hence $\|\delta_i\|=O(v_i)$, and the rates for $\bar\beta_n$, $\Phi_n$ and $W_n$ follow as in Steps~2 and~3 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rate}, using Lemma~\ref{lem:precondLR}(b) and the Lipschitz continuity of $\bar G$ and $\Omega_{\rm LR}$.

\emph{Step 4: functional central limit theorem.} Assume $\kappa>\kappa_L(a)$. We claim that $\varepsilon$ can be chosen in Step~3 with $\varepsilon<\min\{(1-a)/2,(2a-1)/4\}$. It suffices that each lower bound of Step~3 is below both quantities:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt]
\item $(1-a)/\kappa<(1-a)/2$ and $(1-a)/\kappa<(2a-1)/4$, by $\kappa>\kappa(a)$;
\item $2/\kappa-a/2<(1-a)/2$, which is equivalent to $\kappa>4$; and $2/\kappa-a/2<(2a-1)/4$, which is equivalent to $\kappa>8/(4a-1)$ and follows from $\kappa>2/(a-1/2)=4/(2a-1)>8/(4a-1)$;
\item $3/\kappa-1+a/2<(1-a)/2$, which is equivalent to $\kappa>6/(3-2a)$ and follows from $\kappa>6$; and $3/\kappa-1+a/2<(2a-1)/4$, which is equivalent to $\kappa>4$.
\end{itemize}
With such an $\varepsilon$, the bounds used for $R^{(1)}$ and $R^{(4)}$ in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt} hold. For $i>\iota_1$, rearranging the recursion of Step~3 gives
\[
\delta_{i-D}=\frac{\delta_{i-1}-\delta_i}{\gamma_i}-P_{i-D}e_i-\rho_{i-D}-r_i,\qquad\rho_{i-D}=P_{i-D}m(\beta_{i-D})-\delta_{i-D}.
\]
Write $e_i=\xi^0_i+\zeta_i$ with $\xi^0_i=g(X_i,\beta^*)$ and $\zeta_i=g(X_i,\beta_{i-D})-g(X_i,\beta^*)-m(\beta_{i-D})$. By (D1), $\mathbb{E}[\zeta_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta_i\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-D}]\le\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\|\delta_{i-D}\|^2$. Summing over $\iota_1<i\le k$,
\[
\sum_{i=\iota_1+1}^k\delta_{i-D}=-P^*_{\rm LR}\sum_{i=\iota_1+1}^k\xi^0_i+R^{(1)}_k-R^{(2)}_k-R^{(3)}_k-R^{(4)}_k-R^{(5)}_k,
\]
with $R^{(1)}$ as before, $R^{(2)}_k=P^*_{\rm LR}\sum\zeta_i$, $R^{(3)}_k=\sum(P_{i-D}-P^*_{\rm LR})e_i$, $R^{(4)}_k=\sum\rho_{i-D}$ and $R^{(5)}_k=\sum r_i$, all sums over $\iota_1<i\le k$.

The left-hand side equals $\sum_{j=\iota_1+1-D}^{k-D}\delta_j$, whereas $\sum_{i=\iota_1+1}^k\delta_{i-1}=\sum_{j=\iota_1}^{k-1}\delta_j$. The two differ by at most $2(D-1)$ terms, each bounded by $D_\Theta$, which is negligible after division by $\sqrt n$. The terms $R^{(1)}$ and $R^{(4)}$ are bounded as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt}, using $\|\rho_{i-D}\|\le Cv_{i-D}^2\le Cv_i^2$. For $R^{(5)}$, \eqref{eq:rbound} gives
\[
\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}\|r_i\|\le\frac{C(\omega)}{\sqrt n}\Big(1+n^{1-a+2/\kappa}+n^{3/\kappa}\Big)\to0 ,
\]
because $1/2-a+2/\kappa<0$ (as $\kappa>2/(a-1/2)$) and $3/\kappa<1/2$ (as $\kappa>6$). For $R^{(2)}$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(d) with delay $k=D$ to the sequence $P^*_{\rm LR}\zeta_i$, $i>D$, with $\vartheta_{i-D}=C\|\delta_{i-D}\|^2$, whose Ces\`aro averages tend to zero. As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt}, $\max_{k\le n}\|R^{(2)}_k\|$ is at most twice the maximum of the full partial sums. For $R^{(3)}$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:delay}(d) with delay $k=D$ to $(\tilde P_{i-D}-P^*_{\rm LR})e_i$, with $\vartheta_{i-D}=4\mathbb{E}[B(X)^2]\|\tilde P_{i-D}-P^*_{\rm LR}\|^2\to0$, and note that $\tilde P_{i-D}=P_{i-D}$ for $i>\iota_1$. Hence \eqref{eq:bahadur} holds with $P^*_{\rm LR}$ in place of $P^*$.

It remains to show that $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\le\lfloor nt\rfloor}\xi^0_i\Rightarrow\Omega_{\rm LR}^{*1/2}\mathbf B_g$ in $D[0,1]^{d_g}$. Since $P^*_{\rm LR}\Omega^*_{\rm LR}P^{*\top}_{\rm LR}=\Sigma^*_{\rm LR}$, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt} then follows as before. The statement concerns only the distribution of the stationary, $L$-dependent, centred and square-integrable sequence $\xi^0_i$. We may therefore assume, by Kolmogorov's extension theorem, that $(X_i)$ is defined for all $i\in\mathbb Z$, stationary and $L$-dependent. Let $\mathcal H_i=\sigma(X_j:j\le i)$. By $L$-dependence, $\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i+h}\mid\mathcal H_i]=0$ for $h>L$. Define
\[
\upsilon_i=\sum_{h=1}^L\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i+h}\mid\mathcal H_i],\qquad d_i=\sum_{h=0}^L\big(\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i+h}\mid\mathcal H_i]-\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i+h}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]\big).
\]
Then $(d_i)$ is a stationary, square-integrable martingale difference sequence for $(\mathcal H_i)$, and $(\upsilon_i)$ is stationary and square-integrable. Using $\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i+L}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]=0$,
\[
d_i=\xi^0_i+\upsilon_i-\sum_{h=1}^{L+1}\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_{i-1+h}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]=\xi^0_i+\upsilon_i-\upsilon_{i-1},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\xi^0_i=d_i+\upsilon_{i-1}-\upsilon_i .
\]
The coboundary is negligible. For $\eta>0$, stationarity gives
\[
\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{k\le n}\|\upsilon_k\|>\eta\sqrt n\Big)\le n\mathbb{P}(\|\upsilon_0\|>\eta\sqrt n)\le\eta^{-2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|\upsilon_0\|^2\mathbf 1\{\|\upsilon_0\|>\eta\sqrt n\}\big]\to0 ,
\]
so $n^{-1/2}\max_{k\le n}\|\upsilon_0-\upsilon_k\|\to0$ in probability.

The shift is mixing for an $L$-dependent stationary sequence, because events depending on finitely many coordinates become independent of their shifts once the shift exceeds $L$ plus the length of their index window. It is therefore ergodic. The sequence $\mathbb{E}[d_id_i^{\top}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]$ is stationary, so by the ergodic theorem $n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\mathbb{E}[d_id_i^{\top}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]\to\mathbb{E}[d_0d_0^{\top}]$ almost surely. The conditional Lindeberg condition holds because $\mathbb{E}\big[n^{-1}\sum_{i\le n}\mathbb{E}[\|d_i\|^2\mathbf 1\{\|d_i\|>\eta\sqrt n\}\mid\mathcal H_{i-1}]\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\|d_0\|^2\mathbf 1\{\|d_0\|>\eta\sqrt n\}\big]\to0$. By the martingale invariance principle \cite{Brown1971}, applied to $\lambda^{\top} d_i$ for every $\lambda$, together with the Cram\'er--Wold device and coordinatewise tightness, $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i\le\lfloor nt\rfloor}d_i\Rightarrow(\mathbb{E} d_0d_0^{\top})^{1/2}\mathbf B_g$.

Finally, $\mathbb{E}[d_0d_0^{\top}]=\Omega^*_{\rm LR}$. Indeed, $\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{i\le n}\xi^0_i)=\sum_{|h|\le L}(n-|h|)\mathbb{E}[\xi^0_0\xi^{0\top}_h]=n\Omega^*_{\rm LR}+O(1)$. On the other hand, $\sum_{i\le n}\xi^0_i=\sum_{i\le n}d_i+\upsilon_0-\upsilon_n$, whose variance is $n\mathbb{E}[d_0d_0^{\top}]+O(\sqrt n)$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.

\emph{Step 5: inference and the overidentification statistic.} Corollary~\ref{cor:inference} follows from Step~4 and $H_n\to\Sigma^*_{\rm LR}$, with the same proof. In the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:J}, Step~1 uses only the rates of Step~3 with $\varepsilon<(2a-1)/4$ and the strong law for $L(X_i)$, which holds by (D2). In Step~2, $\check G_n\to G^*$ by (D2), and $\sqrt n\,\bar g_n(\beta^*)\Rightarrow N(0,\Omega^*_{\rm LR})$ by Step~4 at $t=1$. The rest of the argument is unchanged with $\Omega^*_{\rm LR}$, $\Sigma^*_{\rm LR}$ and $P^*_{\rm LR}$ in place of $\Omega^*$, $\Sigma^*$ and $P^*$, because $W_n\to\Omega_{\rm LR}^{*-1}$.
